case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a private citizen who has left government employment but still informally exercises governmental power and is slated to return to office owes a fiduciary duty to the public such that he can be convicted of federal honest-services wire fraud.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1346 (honest-services fraud, as incorporated through the federal mail/wire fraud statutes, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1341, 1343).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Percoco argues that honest-services fraud should be limited to clear categories—principally public officials (or those with a formal governmental position) and private employees owing duties to their employers—and that the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory improperly extends § 1346 to politically influential private citizens based on vague, fact-bound notions of influence over government. He contends this expansion provides inadequate notice (due process/vagueness concerns), risks chilling protected political advocacy and association (First Amendment concerns raised by amici), and intrudes on states’ ability to set and enforce their own ethics regimes by converting ordinary lobbying/advocacy into federal crimes whenever prosecutors claim the citizen effectively controlled government decisions.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that § 1346 covers bribery schemes involving individuals who, while not holding the title at the moment, in fact function as government decisionmakers—here, someone who left the payroll temporarily but continued to perform the functions of public office and had been selected to return. On that view, the relevant duty is triggered by de facto exercise of governmental authority and public trust (not merely formal employment status), and limiting liability to only formal officeholders would create an easy loophole for corruption during transition periods or temporary leaves when insiders still wield official power.
key_precedents: McConnell v. FEC, 540 U.S. 93 (2003) (Kennedy, J., concurring in judgment in part and dissenting in part)
United States v. Percoco, 13 F.4th 180 (2d Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains the transition-period “loophole,” but as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress, that policy concern cannot supply the limiting principle Skilling required to save § 1346 from vagueness in criminal prosecutions. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction makes the fiduciary-duty element turn on an amorphous, fact-bound assessment of clout and access, inviting arbitrary enforcement and chilling ordinary political advocacy—precisely what our post-Skilling cases warn against. I agree with Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh that a narrower, administrable boundary exists: liability may attach when there is an objective, preexisting duty to the public “beyond dispute” grounded in formal office, formal delegation, or a recognized agency relationship, and this charge did not require that. Given institutional legitimacy and federalism concerns, we should reverse on the narrow ground that this instruction was overbroad without foreclosing Congress from addressing any interregnum gap with clearer text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s strongest argument—the transition-period “loophole” for powerful private actors—remains a policy concern that cannot supply the limiting principle missing from § 1346’s text, especially after Skilling’s constitutionally compelled narrowing. Chief Justice Roberts correctly emphasizes administrability: the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction makes criminal liability hinge on fact-bound judgments about influence rather than an objective, preexisting fiduciary status or formal agency “beyond dispute,” reintroducing the vagueness Skilling sought to cure. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity point reinforces that any ambiguity about whether a private citizen owes the public “honest services” must be resolved against expansion in a criminal case. Federalism also counsels restraint: absent a clear statement, we should not federalize state political influence and ethics norms through an elastic, judge-made duty concept.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the asserted transition-period “loophole,” but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Skilling’s saving construction relies on a clear fiduciary-duty anchor; the Second Circuit’s reliance-and-control test replaces that with an indeterminate inquiry into clout and access, reviving vagueness and delegating too much discretion to prosecutors and juries. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity concern reinforces that where § 1346’s text provides no principled stopping point for defining a public duty owed by private citizens, we must not expand criminal liability by implication. Even if Percoco’s conduct looks like bribery in a colloquial sense, criminal statutes must provide fair notice and administrable lines, and an influence-based “duty to the public” would chill ordinary political advocacy and risk federalizing state ethics norms without a clear statement. Congress can close any perceived gap with precise language, but we should not do so under the guise of interpretation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains the transition-period “loophole,” but due process and fair notice in criminal law require a clear, administrable fiduciary-duty anchor; otherwise liability turns on pliable judgments about influence that invite arbitrary enforcement and chill ordinary political advocacy. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain that the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction dissolves Skilling’s limiting principle into a fact-bound clout inquiry, recreating the vagueness problems Skilling and McDonnell warned against. I’m open to a narrower path that captures true de facto officials, but only when tied to objective indicia—formal delegation, a recognized agency relationship, or some duty “beyond dispute”—not a jury’s impression of access. Because this charge allowed conviction without that clear duty boundary, reversal is warranted notwithstanding the policy concern.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s best “loophole” argument—that transition-period insiders can sell access while technically off payroll—has force as a policy matter, but it can’t justify extending § 1346 past the administrable fiduciary-duty anchor that saved it in Skilling without reintroducing vagueness. Chief Justice Roberts is right that the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction effectively lets juries infer a public duty from clout and access, which makes criminal liability turn on an indeterminate, fact-bound influence inquiry rather than a clearly preexisting duty. Justice Barrett’s point underscores the textual problem: § 1346 supplies no workable criterion for when a private citizen owes the public “honest services” absent formal delegation or a recognized agency relationship. On a pragmatic textualist view, workable statutory coherence and fair notice require reversal on this jury charge, leaving any true gap for Congress (or clearer statutes) to address.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Government’s “loophole” concern remains the best respondent-side point, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Skilling’s constitutionally necessary narrowing construction depends on a clear, administrable fiduciary-duty anchor—one not satisfied by the Second Circuit’s influence-laden “reliance-and-control” test. That test makes criminal liability turn on amorphous assessments of clout and access, reviving the vagueness and prosecutorial discretion Skilling sought to eliminate and undermining fair notice in a criminal statute. Justice Barrett’s observation that § 1346’s text supplies no principled rule for when a private citizen owes the public “honest services” confirms that any further expansion would be judicial lawmaking, contrary to separation of powers and lenity. If a transition-period gap exists, Congress can close it with clear language; we should not do so by implication in a federal felony case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the “transition-period loophole”: a powerful private actor can effectively run government and sell influence. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Skilling’s constitutionally necessary narrowing depends on a clear, preexisting fiduciary-duty anchor; the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” standard is too indeterminate and fact-bound, risking the very vagueness and discretionary enforcement Skilling rejected. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity point reinforces that, in a criminal statute, any uncertainty about whether a private citizen owes honest services to the public must be resolved against expansion absent objective indicia like formal office, delegation, or a recognized agency relationship. Policy concerns about a gap are for Congress to fix with clearer text, not for us to supply by stretching § 1346 beyond administrable historical limits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—that powerful private actors can effectively run government during transitions—cannot supply the limiting principle § 1346 lacks; under Skilling the statute is constitutionally tolerable only because we confined it to bribery/kickbacks tethered to a fiduciary duty that is clear and preexisting. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern is decisive: the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction makes the duty element turn on amorphous judgments about influence and access, reviving the vagueness and discretionary-enforcement risks Skilling sought to cure. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity point reinforces that, in a criminal statute, any genuine uncertainty about whether a private citizen owes the public “honest services” must be resolved against expansion absent an objective anchor like formal office, delegation, or a recognized agency relationship. Even if a policy gap remains, separation of powers and federalism counsel leaving that to Congress to address with clearer text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s best point remains the transition-period “loophole,” but policy anxiety cannot substitute for the clear fiduciary-duty anchor that Skilling requires to keep § 1346 administrable and consistent with fair notice. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction effectively makes criminal liability turn on perceptions of clout and access, collapsing the duty inquiry into an amorphous influence test that revives the vagueness and discretionary-enforcement problems Skilling sought to cure. From a pragmatic, procedural-fairness perspective, that indeterminacy is especially troubling in criminal prosecutions because it chills ordinary political advocacy and invites uneven application across jurisdictions. I therefore remain persuaded that any gap for transition actors must be addressed through objective indicia of authority (formal delegation/agency) or clearer statutory tools, not by stretching § 1346 beyond its narrowed construction.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358 (2010), § 1346 is constitutional only as narrowly construed to cover bribery or kickback schemes that involve a breach of a clearly defined fiduciary duty, thereby avoiding vagueness. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction risks expanding honest-services fraud beyond the core, historically grounded category of public officials (or clear agents) into a fact-bound inquiry about informal political influence, creating the same notice and line-drawing problems Skilling sought to prevent. A narrower rule better preserves institutional legitimacy by cabining federal criminal liability to situations with a formal or otherwise clearly established governmental duty, leaving states primary responsibility for regulating ordinary political activity and ethics. Because the jury could have convicted on an overbroad theory untethered to a clear fiduciary relationship to the public, the conviction cannot stand as charged under § 1346.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1346’s text—“the intangible right of honest services”—does not define whose “services” are owed or when a private citizen acquires a public fiduciary duty, and this Court in Skilling v. United States limited § 1346 to the core of bribery-and-kickback schemes precisely to avoid vagueness and boundless prosecutorial discretion. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory extends honest-services liability beyond clear, historically grounded fiduciary-duty categories (public officeholders and private employees/agents) to politically connected citizens based on amorphous influence, raising the same due-process notice concerns Skilling sought to cure. If Congress wishes to criminalize informal political influence by non-officeholders, it must do so with clear text rather than by stretching § 1346 through judicial construction. Federalism concerns also counsel restraint where States retain primary authority over regulating state political actors and ethics absent a clear federal command.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1346, as construed in Skilling v. United States, reaches only bribery-and-kickback schemes that are anchored in a clear, preexisting fiduciary duty; extending that duty to a politically influential private citizen based on an amorphous “reliance-and-control” theory lacks a principled textual or historical stopping point. The Second Circuit’s approach risks the vagueness concerns Skilling avoided by narrowing § 1346, because it makes criminal liability turn on fact-bound perceptions of influence rather than a defined legal status or agency relationship. A limiting rule tied to formal officeholding or a recognized agency relationship also avoids converting ordinary political advocacy and access into federal felonies and better respects federalism by not federalizing state ethics norms through an indeterminate fiduciary-duty concept. Because petitioner was not a public official at the relevant time, the conviction cannot rest on § 1346 absent a clearly established duty comparable to traditional public-office or private-employment fiduciary obligations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1346, as narrowed in Skilling v. United States, reaches only bribery and kickback schemes that involve a breach of a fiduciary duty, and the duty line must be administrable enough to give fair notice and prevent arbitrary enforcement. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory risks collapsing that duty requirement into a vague, influence-based standard that can sweep in ordinary political advocacy or lobbying by private citizens, raising serious due process concerns even if the underlying conduct is unsavory. While the Government’s concern about a loophole during transition periods is real, Congress has provided other, clearer anti-corruption tools, and expanding § 1346 beyond formal or clearly defined agency-like relationships threatens to federalize state ethics and chill protected political association. On this record, I would require a more definite public fiduciary status than informal influence to sustain an honest-services conviction under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1343 and 1346.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Skilling v. United States, 18 U.S.C. § 1346 is saved from vagueness only by a limiting construction tied to bribery/kickbacks involving a clearly defined fiduciary duty, and the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” instruction risks turning informal political influence into a federal duty of “honest services” without a workable, administrable boundary. The text of § 1346 speaks in terms of “honest services,” but Skilling makes the duty element doing the real limiting work; extending that duty to private citizens based on fact-bound assessments of influence and access would reintroduce the due process notice problems Skilling sought to avoid. While the Government’s loophole concern is real, it can be addressed by anchoring liability to objective indicia of governmental authority (e.g., formal delegation or agency), rather than a nebulous de facto-control theory that would chill ordinary advocacy and blur state ethics lines. Because the jury charge here allowed conviction without that clear limiting principle, the conviction cannot stand on this theory.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1346’s text—“the intangible right of honest services”—does not itself specify who owes what fiduciary duty, and in Skilling v. United States the Court upheld the statute only by adopting a narrowing construction limited to bribe-and-kickback schemes that violate clear, preexisting fiduciary duties “beyond dispute.” Extending § 1346 to a private citizen based on an amorphous “reliance-and-control” theory invites the very vagueness and prosecutorial discretion Skilling sought to avoid, and it risks criminalizing ordinary political influence without a clear statutory hook. If Congress wishes to reach former or future officials on leave, it must do so with precision; federal courts should not expand § 1346 beyond its narrowed, historically grounded core in a way that compromises fair notice and separation of powers. At minimum, uncertainty about whether a private citizen in petitioner’s posture owes a fiduciary duty to “the public” triggers the rule-of-lenity principle against stretching criminal statutes by implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358 (2010), § 1346 must be confined to bribery/kickback schemes that involve a clear, established fiduciary duty, adopted as a limiting construction to avoid vagueness and provide fair notice. Extending honest-services liability to a private citizen based on the Second Circuit’s fact-bound “reliance-and-control” theory risks recreating the indeterminacy Skilling rejected, because it turns on informal influence rather than a formal office, agency relationship, or other duty “beyond dispute.” Practical workability and institutional concerns counsel against a federal criminal standard that would invite inconsistent enforcement and chill ordinary political advocacy by making liability hinge on perceived clout. If Congress wishes to reach this transition-period conduct, it can do so with a more precise statute than § 1346 as narrowed in Skilling.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1346, as construed in Skilling v. United States, reaches only bribery-and-kickback schemes that involve a breach of a fiduciary duty, and we must interpret that duty with narrow, administrable boundaries to avoid vagueness in a criminal statute. The Second Circuit’s “domination and control/reliance” test turns honest-services liability on indeterminate assessments of political influence, risking inadequate notice and chilling ordinary advocacy, and it is difficult to square with our insistence on clear limiting principles in cases like McDonnell v. United States. Textually, nothing in § 1346 supplies a standard for when a private citizen—without formal office—owes the public “honest services,” and federalism counsels against converting state political practices into federal felonies absent a clear congressional statement. Percoco could be prosecuted under valid theories tied to formal agency or official action, but this expansive instruction cannot stand and requires reversal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358 (2010), § 1346 is saved from vagueness only by a limiting construction that ties honest-services fraud to bribery or kickbacks that breach a clearly defined fiduciary duty; expanding that duty to a private citizen based on an amorphous “reliance-and-control” theory risks reviving the very vagueness and fair-notice problems Skilling sought to avoid. A rule that turns informal political influence and anticipated return to office into a public fiduciary obligation lacks administrable boundaries and creates serious practical consequences, including chilling legitimate advocacy and enabling uneven enforcement. While the government has a strong interest in preventing corruption during transition periods, Congress has provided other tools for public corruption, and § 1346 should not be stretched beyond clear, procedurally fair categories without a formal governmental position or agency relationship. Given due process concerns and the need for clear lines in criminal law, the conviction cannot rest on the Second Circuit’s expansive theory.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a private citizen who has formally left government employment but continues to wield de facto governmental power (and is expected to return) owes the public a fiduciary duty enforceable through the federal honest-services fraud statute.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1346 (honest-services fraud, as a definition of “scheme or artifice to defraud” in the mail/wire fraud statutes); relatedly 18 U.S.C. §§ 1341, 1343 (mail/wire fraud framework) and constitutional due process/First Amendment concerns raised by amici about vagueness and chilling political activity.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Percoco argues that honest-services fraud liability should be limited to actual public officials (or at least persons holding an official position with clear, legally defined duties) and cannot rest on the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory—i.e., that any private citizen who is influential, “relied on” by government, and in practice “controls” government business thereby owes a fiduciary duty to the public. He (and supporting amici) contend that this theory is dangerously indeterminate, expands federal criminal law beyond recognized bribery/kickback boundaries, provides inadequate notice of what conduct is criminal, intrudes on states’ authority to set ethical rules for their own officials, and risks chilling constitutionally protected political advocacy and engagement.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that honest-services duties can extend beyond formal title where an individual, though out of office in name, continues in fact to perform governmental functions and exercise the powers of public office—especially where the person has been selected to return to the role. On that view, when a defendant acts as a functional government decisionmaker, he is obliged to provide honest services (i.e., not be corrupted by bribes/kickbacks) just like a formal officeholder, and the conviction can be sustained because the defendant’s conduct fits within § 1346 as properly limited to bribery/kickback corruption.
key_precedents: Citizens United v. FEC, 558 U.S. 310 (2010) (quoted for concern about unbounded “influence” theories and First Amendment limits)
McConnell v. FEC, 540 U.S. 93 (2003) (Kennedy, J., quoted via Citizens United)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—the “functional official” theory—captures a real corruption concern, but it still makes liability under § 1346 turn on indeterminate judgments about influence and access, recreating the vagueness Skilling narrowed the statute to avoid. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on McDonnell underscores why we need clear, administrable limiting principles in public-corruption cases; the Second Circuit’s reliance-and-control test does not provide that ex ante notice. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity and separation-of-powers framing reinforces that we should not extend a federal criminal statute to novel fiduciary duties untethered to formal office or a well-settled agency relationship. A narrow reversal on that ground preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves any broader coverage to Congress or state law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s best point is the “functional official” theory—that a private actor who effectively wields state power should not be able to sell it—but that contention has no foothold in § 1346’s text and would revive the indeterminacy Skilling rejected. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh correctly emphasize that the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” standard makes criminal liability turn on amorphous judgments about influence and access, not a determinate, legally defined fiduciary duty capable of giving fair notice. Justice Gorsuch’s invocation of lenity and separation of powers strengthens the textualist conclusion: absent formal office, employment, or a well-settled agency relationship, courts have no authority to fabricate a “duty to the public” for private citizens. Federalism confirms the point—if States or Congress wish to criminalize this kind of private political brokerage, they must do so with unmistakable clarity rather than through an elastic honest-services theory.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Government’s best point is the “functional official” theory—that someone who effectively wields governmental power should not be able to sell it with impunity—but § 1346, after Skilling, cannot turn criminal liability on a jury’s impressionistic assessment of influence and access rather than a clearly defined fiduciary source. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” standard reintroduces the very vagueness and lack of fair notice Skilling narrowed § 1346 to avoid, and that indeterminacy carries serious practical consequences: it invites arbitrary enforcement and chills ordinary political advocacy. Justice Kavanaugh’s McDonnell analogy reinforces that we insist on clear limiting principles in corruption prosecutions; expanding honest-services fraud to de facto power untethered to formal office or a well-settled agency relationship would effectively recreate a common-law corruption statute. Federalism and separation-of-powers concerns counsel leaving any broader coverage of powerful private actors to Congress or the States to define with precision, not to federal prosecutors through elastic fiduciary-duty theories.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—that a private actor can wield real governmental power and selling it is paradigmatic corruption—has force, but in criminal law we cannot let liability turn on a jury’s after-the-fact sense of “influence.” Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Skilling’s due-process demand for a clear, administrable fiduciary-duty anchor is decisive for me: the Second Circuit’s reliance-and-control test is too elastic and risks arbitrary enforcement that would chill ordinary advocacy and community organizing. Justice Kavanaugh’s analogy to McDonnell reinforces that we require limiting principles in public-corruption cases precisely to protect notice and prevent prosecutors from turning “access” into a crime. Other statutes may cover quid pro quo corruption here, but stretching § 1346 to de facto power untethered to formal office or a settled agency relationship revives the vagueness Skilling was meant to cure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The government’s strongest point—its “functional official” theory—has intuitive appeal because it targets obvious corruption, but in a criminal statute the duty element cannot hinge on an open-ended, jury-driven assessment of “influence” and “access.” Chief Justice Roberts is right that Skilling’s vagueness-avoidance narrowing requires a determinate fiduciary-duty source, and the Second Circuit’s reliance-and-control test supplies no clear, legally grounded boundary; it risks reintroducing the indeterminacy Skilling cured. Justice Kavanaugh’s McDonnell analogy reinforces that we have repeatedly insisted on limiting principles to avoid chilling ordinary political engagement and arbitrary enforcement, and this theory lacks that administrable line. I therefore remain persuaded that § 1346, as narrowed, covers bribery/kickbacks only where a formal office, employment, or similarly well-settled agency relationship establishes the fiduciary duty ex ante.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The government’s best point—emphasized by the Chief Justice—is the “functional official” intuition: if a private actor in fact runs government, selling that power looks like bribery and should be punishable. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Skilling’s narrowing construction did not simply bless prosecuting “bribery” in the abstract; it preserved bribery/kickbacks only when tethered to a clearly defined fiduciary duty, and the Second Circuit’s reliance-and-control test replaces that legal anchor with a jury’s impression of influence and access. That approach reintroduces the very indeterminacy and notice problems that Skilling and McDonnell sought to avoid, and lenity plus separation-of-powers principles forbid us from expanding § 1346 to create a new, amorphous public fiduciary duty for private citizens. If Congress wishes to criminalize this category of conduct, it must do so with a clear rule rather than leaving the boundary to prosecutors and juries.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s best point is the “functional official” theory—real power can be sold just like formal power—but that functionalism does not solve the due-process problem; it just relocates it to a jury’s ad hoc assessment of “influence,” “access,” and “control.” As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Skilling’s vagueness-avoidance narrowing requires an administrable, legally grounded fiduciary-duty anchor, and the Second Circuit’s reliance-and-control test risks reviving the very indeterminacy Skilling rejected. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity/separation-of-powers point reinforces that we should not expand § 1346 beyond duties “beyond dispute” absent formal office or a clearly defined agency relationship, especially given the chilling and arbitrary-enforcement concerns we flagged in McDonnell and Kelly. The appropriate institutionalist course is a narrow rule reversing here and leaving any broader extension to Congress or the States with clear lines.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains functional: a private actor who effectively controls government decisions can sell public power in a way that looks like classic bribery. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Skilling’s narrowing construction is a notice-protecting, vagueness-avoidance move that depends on a clear, legally grounded fiduciary-duty source; the Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” test makes that duty turn on amorphous assessments of influence and expectations. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of McDonnell reinforces that we need administrable limiting principles in corruption prosecutions to avoid chilling ordinary political engagement, and this theory risks recreating the indeterminate honest-services regime Skilling rejected. Under a textualist/originalist approach, absent formal office, employment, or a well-settled agency relationship, § 1346 cannot be extended to de facto power without raising serious due process and separation-of-powers concerns that Congress—not courts—must resolve.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s best point remains the “functional official” intuition—if someone effectively runs government, selling that power looks like bribery—but that framing does not answer Skilling’s due-process problem: § 1346 can’t hinge on a jury’s post hoc sense of influence rather than a preexisting, legally defined fiduciary duty. As Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, Skilling’s narrowing was not “bribery anywhere near government,” but bribery/kickbacks in the context of an administrable duty that provides fair notice; the Second Circuit’s reliance-and-control test recreates the same vagueness and arbitrariness concerns we highlighted in McDonnell and Kelly. Justice Gorsuch’s lenity point reinforces the practical consequence here: expanding honest-services fraud to informal political actors would chill ordinary advocacy and invite selective enforcement, especially in contexts where access is the only available avenue to be heard. Nothing in the respondent’s functional theory supplies a clear limiting principle comparable to formal office, employment, or a well-settled agency relationship, so the conviction cannot stand under § 1346 as construed.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1346 must be construed narrowly to avoid the vagueness and notice concerns this Court identified in Skilling v. United States, which limited honest-services fraud to bribery and kickback schemes anchored in a clear fiduciary duty. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory makes criminal liability turn on indeterminate concepts like influence and informal access rather than a legally defined office or agency relationship, inviting the very unpredictability Skilling sought to prevent and risking chilling of ordinary political engagement. Because Congress has not clearly extended § 1346 to private citizens based on de facto power alone, federalism and institutional legitimacy counsel against expanding federal criminal law through judicially created standards. The conviction cannot rest on a theory that fails to provide a clear, administrable boundary for when a private citizen owes the public a fiduciary duty.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1346’s text defines a “scheme or artifice to defraud” to include depriving another of “the intangible right of honest services,” but it does not specify who owes that duty; expanding it to private citizens based on an indeterminate “reliance-and-control” theory lacks a clear textual anchor and risks arbitrary enforcement. In Skilling v. United States, 561 U.S. 358 (2010), the Court adopted a narrowing construction to avoid vagueness by limiting § 1346 to bribery and kickback schemes, yet that limitation still presupposes a legally cognizable fiduciary duty—something not supplied by mere political influence or informal power. Allowing federal prosecutors to criminalize state political activity whenever an influential private actor is “relied on” by officials intrudes on state authority to define offices and ethical obligations and raises serious due process and First Amendment chilling concerns. Because the Second Circuit’s theory lacks a determinate, historically grounded boundary consistent with the original public meaning and Skilling’s vagueness-avoidance rationale, the conviction cannot rest on it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1346, as construed in Skilling v. United States, reaches only bribery-and-kickback schemes that involve the breach of a clearly defined fiduciary duty; importing the Second Circuit’s indeterminate “reliance-and-control” test would reintroduce the very vagueness and overbreadth problems Skilling sought to cure. A private citizen’s “influence” or expected return to government is not, by itself, a textual or historically grounded source of a fiduciary duty to “the public” comparable to the duties of an actual officeholder or an established agent. Expanding § 1346 to cover de facto power untethered to formal office or a clear agency relationship risks chilling ordinary political advocacy and invites unpredictable prosecutions, raising serious due process and First Amendment concerns (cf. Citizens United’s skepticism of amorphous influence theories). The conviction therefore cannot rest on this theory without exceeding § 1346’s limiting construction and compromising fair notice.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1346 can be sustained only under the narrowing construction adopted in Skilling v. United States, which limits honest-services fraud to bribery and kickback schemes that breach a fiduciary duty that is “beyond dispute.” Extending federal criminal liability to a private citizen based on an indeterminate “reliance-and-control” theory—untethered to a clear office, appointment, or legally defined duty—revives the vagueness and arbitrary-enforcement risks Skilling sought to cure and threatens to chill ordinary political advocacy, implicating due process and First Amendment concerns. While corruption that exploits real governmental power is a serious harm, fairness and access to justice require clear notice of who owes the public a fiduciary duty; that boundary cannot turn on perceived influence alone. The government may prosecute bribery through other clearly defined statutes, but § 1346 should not be stretched beyond Skilling’s core without a concrete, formal duty to the public.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1346, as narrowed in Skilling v. United States, reaches only bribery-and-kickback schemes that involve a violation of a fiduciary duty, and that fiduciary-duty anchor must be sufficiently clear to satisfy due process notice concerns. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory risks criminalizing indistinct categories of political influence and access, untethered to any formal office or legally defined governmental duty, raising the same vagueness and chilling concerns that drove Skilling’s limiting construction. While the government’s “functional official” theory may sometimes describe real-world power, § 1346 is a criminal statute and should not be extended by an indeterminate standard better left to state ethics regimes or to Congress to define with precision. Because the conviction here rests on an overbroad duty theory rather than a clearly established fiduciary relationship akin to a public office or agency, it cannot stand under § 1346 and the mail/wire fraud framework (18 U.S.C. §§ 1341, 1343).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1346, on its face, does not define who owes the public “honest services,” and after Skilling v. United States it may be applied only to bribery-and-kickback schemes that involve the breach of a clearly established fiduciary duty. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” test turns criminal liability on an amorphous assessment of “influence” and informal access, raising the very vagueness and notice concerns Skilling sought to avoid and inviting inconsistent application that chills ordinary political activity. In criminal law we insist on clear lines drawn by Congress, not federal courts, and the rule of lenity counsels against extending § 1346 to private citizens lacking a formal, legally defined public office or agency relationship. Expanding honest-services duties based on de facto power also risks displacing States’ authority to define and police their own officials’ ethical obligations, contrary to basic separation-of-powers and federalism principles.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1346 must be construed narrowly to avoid vagueness and arbitrary enforcement, and under Skilling v. United States it is limited to bribery-and-kickback schemes tied to a clearly defined fiduciary duty. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory would extend that duty to influential private citizens without a formal office or legally ascertainable obligations, reviving the indeterminate “good government” theory rejected after McNally and raising serious due process and First Amendment concerns about chilling ordinary political advocacy. Consistent with McDonnell’s insistence on clear limiting principles in public-corruption prosecutions and with principles of judicial restraint and federalism, the Court should not allow § 1346 to criminalize conduct based on amorphous “influence” rather than a formal governmental position or agency relationship. If Congress wishes to reach such conduct, it must do so with a more precise statute than the reliance-and-control test adopted below.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1346 defines a “scheme or artifice to defraud” in terms of “the intangible right of honest services,” but it does not specify who owes that duty; given the serious vagueness concerns inherent in such an open-ended concept, Skilling v. United States limited § 1346 to bribery-and-kickback schemes that violate fiduciary duties “beyond dispute.” 561 U.S. 358, 404, 407 (2010). The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory—turning a private citizen’s influence and informal role into a public fiduciary duty—lacks a clear textual or historically grounded limiting principle and risks resurrecting the indeterminacy Skilling rejected, raising due process and First Amendment chilling concerns. Absent a formal office or legally defined agency relationship establishing fiduciary obligations to the public, extending § 1346 to a de facto-influence theory is not a methodologically consistent, textually anchored application of the statute as narrowed by Skilling.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1346 can be sustained only under Skilling’s limiting construction to “core” bribery/kickback schemes tied to clear, settled fiduciary duties, adopted to cure serious vagueness and fair-notice problems under the Due Process Clause. The Second Circuit’s “reliance-and-control” theory effectively makes criminal liability turn on amorphous influence and informal access rather than a legally defined duty, risking arbitrary enforcement and chilling ordinary political advocacy—concerns this Court has repeatedly flagged when constraining public-corruption prosecutions (Skilling; see also Kelly and McDonnell’s emphasis on clear lines). Because Percoco was a private citizen without a formal office or other well-defined source of fiduciary obligation, extending honest-services liability here would expand § 1346 beyond the “beyond dispute” duties Skilling contemplated and undermine procedural fairness. The conviction should therefore be reversed absent a showing of a clear, preexisting fiduciary duty comparable to that of an actual public official or employee.
